name: Metal weight
seoDesc: Metal weight: work out total weight (Result) from the length and the width. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the length, the width, the side length and the outer radius and the Metal weight calculator solves for total weight (Result). Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Metal weight calculator work?
sections.html:
The Metal weight calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total weight (Result) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the alloy and metal options and the shape); then you type in the length (Dimensions and quantity), the length (Dimensions and quantity), the length (Dimensions and quantity) and the width.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Metal weight calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total weight=material's density × length × number of metal pieces × thickness × width
Side length=(1 ÷ 3) × the square root of (2) × (3 ^ 1 ÷ 4) × the square root of (total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces × thickness))
Radius (r)=the square root of (total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces × thickness)) ÷ the square root of (PI)
Total weight=2 × material's density × number of metal pieces × (side length ^ 2) × thickness × (1 + the square root of (2))
Outer radius (R)=(-4 ÷ 3 × (2) × (PI ^ 8 ÷ 3) × (inner radius (r) ^ 2) + (1 ÷ 3) × (PI ^ 2) × inner radius (r) × (16 × (PI ^ 2) × (inner radius (r) ^ 3) + 3 × the square root of (3) × the square root of (total weight × (-32 × (PI ^ 2) × (inner radius (r) ^ 3) + 27 × total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)) ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)) − 27 × total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)) − 1 ÷ 6 × (PI ^ 4 ÷ 3) × (32 × (PI ^ 2) × (inner radius (r) ^ 3) + 6 × the square root of (3) × the square root of (total weight × (-32 × (PI ^ 2) × (inner radius (r) ^ 3) + 27 × total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)) ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)) − 54 × total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces), 2 ÷ 3)) ÷ ((PI ^ 2) × (16 × (PI ^ 2) × (inner radius (r) ^ 3) + 3 × the square root of (3) × the square root of (total weight × (-32 × (PI ^ 2) × (inner radius (r) ^ 3) + 27 × total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)) ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)) − 27 × total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)))
Volume=total weight ÷ (material's density × number of metal pieces)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Alloy and metal options set to Steel, Material's density = 10 kg/m³, Shape set to Rectangular prism (plate) and Thickness = 30 m. The calculator returns Side length = 35.819 m.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Side length = 35.819 m should be roughly the size you expected from Alloy and metal options set to Steel and Material's density = 10 kg/m³.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Length, opening in meters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Metal weight calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length, the width and the side length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Metal weight calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total weight (Result), derived from the length, the width and the side length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Metal weight calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length, the width, the side length and the outer radius, which is 28 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter material's density in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Material's density opens in kilograms per cubic meter and the chip beside it offers 9 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Side length = 35.819 m. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Metal weight calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
